title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in Austin: Route Engine ⚡
description: Watch Bidirectional Dijkstra split the search from start and goal, meeting in the middle to cut work while preserving shortest-path guarantees. This city-grid visualization shows why modern route planners scale better than one-way search.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional Dijkstra: How Modern Route Planners Scale — Inside high-scale navigation engines: ⚡ Bidirectional Dijkstra visualised.

In today’s Austin routing sim, we run TWO Dijkstra frontiers: one expands from the start, the other from the destination. As soon as the waves meet, we stitch the route using the best known distance—dramatically reducing explored nodes compared to classic single-source Dijkstra.

🔍 What makes it work?
- Same edge weights assumption as Dijkstra (non-negative costs)
- Priority queues drive expansions in increasing distance order (forward + backward)
- A stopping condition prevents wasting compute after an optimal meeting point is proven

✅ Takeaway: Bidirectional search often turns “explore the whole map” into “explore just enough,” which is why route planning engines love it at scale.

🤔 Debate question: Should route planners prioritize fewer expansions (speed) or more uniform exploration (fairness/consistent latency under load)?
